To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the standard test of decisional separabilty is not identifiable, (2) the standard test for decisional separability has high rates of false-positive results, (3) the standard test is not identifiable in any model, and (4) the standard test has high rates of incorrect rejection of the null hypothesis.

(a) decisional separability, which has been the primary inferential tool in GRT, is not identifiable in a common model, (b) tests of perceptual interactions that do not involve marginal signal detection parameters are not identifiable in a second common model, (c) tests based on marginal parameters are not reliable, and (d) the implications of these problems are far-reaching.

(a) failure of decisional separation is unidentifiable in the Gaussian GART model with either of the two common response selection mechanisms, and (b) tests based on marginal sensitivity and bias parameters produce unacceptablly high rates of false positives.

the problem of model identification, which is a fundamental concern in the study of multidimensional perception and response selection.
statistical inference in the context of the general recognition theory.
the problem of testing the statistical significance of perceptual and response selection interactions in full factorial identification paradigms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the GRT framework is a useful tool for the study of perceptual and response selection, but that the framework has serious limitations that should be taken into account in the design and interpretation of experiments.
the GRT framework, as currently formulated, does not provide a viable approach to the study of perceptual and response selection interactions in full-factorial identification.
, for a given data set, the null hypothesis of decisional separabilty is not identifiable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the GRT approach to testing for interactions between perceptual dimensions and response selection is not well suited to the task, and we should look elsewhere for methods to address this problem.
, for the Gaussian GRT framework with two common response selection mechanisms, decisional separability does not identify the failure of perceptual separability.
the GRT approach to multidimensional identification is in need of a major overhaul.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the standard GRT model with Gaussian noise, the two most common response selection models, and the standard tests of perceptual separability are all inadequate to the task of identifying perceptual and decision processes in multidimensional identification.

researchers should not assume that the standard tests of decisional separabilities and perceptual interactions can be used to make strong claims about the relationship between dimensions in identification and categorization.
the standard GRT-based methods for testing perceptual and decisionality interactions in multidimensional recognition tasks are not viable.
